standard.title: Ideas That Influenced Change During the Industrial Revolution
standard.description: the ideas that emerged and influenced change in society, such as nationalism, capitalism, imperialism, socialism, egalitarianism and Chartism
standard.prior_knowledge: Students have examined the causes, effects, and human experiences of the Industrial Revolution (AC9HH9K13–K16). They understand the structural and experiential dimensions of industrialisation. This descriptor asks them to examine the ideational dimension — how new ideas emerged from and responded to industrial conditions, and how these ideas produced political and social change.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students explain the ideas that emerged during the Industrial Revolution and describe how they influenced change in society.

nodes.label: Why ideas emerge — basis and context
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain why specific ideas emerged during the Industrial Revolution, connecting the basis of each idea to the social and economic conditions that made it persuasive.
nodes.minimum_width: Explain why one idea emerged during the Industrial Revolution and describe the social conditions that made it persuasive.
nodes.typical_width: Explain why ideas emerged and the basis of those ideas — including: Chartism (democratic representation for working class); capitalism (private ownership, free markets); socialism (collective ownership, workers' rights); nationalism (political unity based on shared culture/ethnicity); egalitarianism (equal rights and opportunities); imperialism (expansion of empire as economic and political strategy); connect each idea to the industrial conditions that generated it.
wider: Examine how capitalism and socialism emerged as directly competing responses to the same industrial conditions — analysing how Adam Smith and Karl Marx both responded to industrialisation but drew fundamentally different conclusions

Investigate how nationalist ideas spread beyond Britain to Europe and the Americas, examining how the French Revolution and Industrial Revolution together created the ideological conditions for 19th century nationalism
Examine Chartism in detail — identifying the six points of the People's Charter, the social composition of the movement, and why some demands were eventually realised and others were not
nodes.hinge_reason: Understanding that ideas emerge from conditions — rather than appearing spontaneously — is the conceptual move this descriptor requires. Without this, students list ideas without explaining them. The why question is the core analytical demand.

response_modes.reason: Students need an explicit model of how conditions generate ideas before applying it independently. The capitalism/socialism pairing is particularly useful — same conditions, opposing conclusions — as a demonstration of how historical context shapes but does not determine ideological response.

success_criteria: Explains at least three ideas that emerged during the Industrial Revolution, with the social or economic conditions that produced each
Connects the basis of at least two ideas to specific industrial or political conditions, not just abstract principles

nodes.label: The French Revolution and Chartism as examples of ideational change
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can examine the causes and impacts of the French Revolution on politics and citizens' rights, and explain how Chartism applied democratic ideals in the industrial context.
nodes.minimum_width: Describe one change that arose from either the French Revolution or Chartism, explaining how the idea produced the change.
nodes.typical_width: Examine the causes and impacts of the French Revolution on politics and citizens' rights including in Britain and the USA; explain why Chartism emerged and what changes it sought; identify changes that arose from Chartist agitation (universal male suffrage, secret ballot); examine the role of religious beliefs in reform movements (abolition of slavery, workers' rights, women's enfranchisement, organised labour).
wider: Examine how the ideals of the French Revolution (liberty, equality, fraternity) both inspired and frightened the British ruling class — tracing how British political reform was partly shaped by the desire to prevent revolution
Investigate the role of religious nonconformism (Quakers, Methodists) in driving abolition and social reform — examining how religious conviction translated into political activism
Examine the transatlantic connections between Chartism and American abolitionism — tracing how reform ideas crossed borders through the movement of people and publications

response_modes.reason: Using both the French Revolution and Chartism as case studies — along with the role of religion in reform — gives students multiple examples of how ideas lead to political change through different mechanisms and in different contexts.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The relationship between ideas and political change is historically rich and analytically significant — examining how the same ideas (liberty, democratic representation, workers' rights) operated in different contexts (France, Britain, the USA) develops transferable historical thinking about how ideology becomes action.
success_criteria: Describes the impact of the French Revolution on political rights in at least one nation beyond France
Explains how Chartism connected industrial conditions to democratic demands, identifying at least two specific changes sought
